title: To panic or not to panic
summary: Guidelines for choosing between panic! and Result, when unwrap is fine, and how to use types to make invalid values impossible, with the Guess example.

sections: TRPL 9.3 To panic! or Not to panic!
TRPL 9.3 Examples, Prototype Code, and Tests
TRPL 9.3 Cases in Which You Have More Information Than the Compiler

blocks.md: When code fails, should it panic or return a `Result`? Returning a `Result` is the default choice, because it lets the **caller** decide: retry, use a default, report it, or panic after all. Panicking takes that decision away. There are still good reasons to panic, and this lesson lists them.

blocks.title: Guidelines (The Rust Programming Language)
rows: Error handling would obscure the point; a panic in a test is how it fails
You know more than the compiler: the value cannot be invalid
`"127.0.0.1".parse::<IpAddr>()` can only fail if your literal is wrong, a bug
Bad state: a broken assumption, invariant or contract
Continuing would be insecure or harmful; it is a bug for the caller to fix
Failure is expected: parsing input, I/O, network
It will happen in normal use, so the caller must be able to handle it
Calling external code that returns an invalid state you cannot fix

blocks.title: Contracts
blocks.md: A function's **contract** is what it requires from callers. Breaking a contract is a caller's bug, and panicking with a clear message is right: `Vec::remove(i)` panics when `i` is out of range rather than returning a `Result` that every caller would have to check. Document such panics in a `# Panics` section of the doc comment.

blocks.title: Let the type system check for you
blocks.md:
Checking for errors everywhere is tedious. Rust's types can do much of it. A function taking `u32` never needs to check for negative numbers. A function taking `&str` instead of `Option<&str>` never needs to check for a missing value. Push this further with your own types: validate a value **once**, when it is created, and from then on every function that receives the type can rely on it.

In chapter 2's guessing game, the guess must be between 1 and 100. Instead of checking that in every function, make a `Guess` type that cannot hold anything else:

blocks.explain: Because `value` is private, code outside the module cannot write `Guess { value: 500 }`. Every `Guess` in the program has been through `new`, so functions that take a `Guess` need no checks. `new` panics because, in this design, passing an out-of-range number is the caller's bug. When the number comes straight from a user, offer a fallible constructor instead, as the exercise does.

blocks.title: A fallible constructor
blocks.md: Add `Percent::try_new(value: u8) -> Result<Percent, String>`, returning an error message for values above 100 instead of panicking, and use it in `main`.
hints: `if value > 100 { return Err(format!("{value} is more than 100")); }` then `Ok(Percent(value))`.

blocks.title: Validated types
blocks.goal: Create types whose constructors check the rules once, so the rest of the code can trust them.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub struct Username(String)` with `pub fn parse(s: &str) -> Result<Username, String>`: 3 to 16 chars after trimming, only ASCII letters, digits and `_`, and not starting with a digit. Errors: `"too short"`, `"too long"`, `"invalid character: <c>"`, `"starts with a digit"` (check in that order). `pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str`.
- `pub struct Guess(i32)` with `pub fn new(v: i32) -> Guess` that panics with a message containing `"between 1 and 100"` when out of range, and `pub fn value(&self) -> i32`.
hints: `for c in s.chars() { if !(c.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || c == '_') { return Err(format!("invalid character: {c}")); } }`
`s.chars().next().unwrap().is_ascii_digit()` is safe once you know the length is at least 3.
blocks.solution_explain: `Username` returns a `Result` because user input is expected to be wrong sometimes; `Guess::new` panics because, by its documented contract, an out-of-range value is the caller's bug. `#[should_panic(expected = ...)]` in the tests checks the panic message; chapter 11 covers it.

questions.q: A function parses a date typed by a user. What should it return on bad input?
questions.explanation: Bad input is expected; let the caller decide.

questions.q: When is `.expect("...")` appropriate in production code?
options: When failure would mean a bug, such as parsing a hard-coded valid literal
questions.explanation: You know more than the compiler; document why in the message.

options: So the only way to create a Guess is `new`, which validates it
questions.explanation: Then every `Guess` is known to be valid.

questions.q: In tests, using `unwrap()` is fine because a panic makes the test fail with a clear location.
questions.explanation: That is exactly how test failures are reported.

points: Default to `Result`: it lets the caller choose what to do.
Panic for bugs: broken contracts, impossible states, failures that make continuing unsafe.
`unwrap`/`expect` are fine in examples, prototypes, tests, and when you can prove failure is impossible.
Validate once in a constructor and keep fields private, so the type itself guarantees the rule.
Document panics in a `# Panics` section.

terms.def: The conditions a function requires of its callers; violating it is the caller's bug.
A condition that is always true for every value of a type, such as a Guess being between 1 and 100.
A type whose constructor checks a rule, so every value of the type is known to satisfy it.
